# ECDF

### What {-}

The empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) gives the proportion of observations at or below $x$.
$$\hat{F}(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}(\hat{X}_{i} \leq x).$$
It is a step function: each observation contributes a jump of $1/n$.

Consider the sample $\hat{X}_{i} \in \{2, 3.1, 0.01\}$.
The ECDF at $0.5$ and $3.5$ is:
\begin{eqnarray*}
x = 0.5 & ~\text{~only $0.01$ is at or below~}~ & \hat{F}(0.5) = 1/3 \\
x = 3.5 & ~\text{~everything is below~}~        & \hat{F}(3.5) = 1
\end{eqnarray*}

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
# Tiny sample to read by hand
X_tiny <- c(2, 3.1, 0.01)
# ECDF of the tiny sample
plot(ecdf(X_tiny), main=NA, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
    xlab='x', ylab='Proportion at or below x')
# Tick marks at each observation
rug(X_tiny)
```

### Why {-}

Histograms show skewness and the number and location of modes more clearly.
But they don't make precise comparisons easy and also need a bandwidth.
The ECDF also has the same definition for discrete and continuous data.



### How {-}

The data are monthly earnings, in 1980 dollars, of 935 US workers from Blackburn and Neumark (1992).
They come from the `wooldridge` package, which you install once with `install.packages('wooldridge')`.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Data
X <- wooldridge::wage2[, 'wage']
# Data summary
F_hat <- ecdf(X)
plot(F_hat, main=NA, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
    xlab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)',
    ylab='Proportion of workers at or below x')
```

Each observation contributes a jump of $1/935$.
Where several workers earn the same amount, such as exactly $1000$ dollars, the jump is larger.
The value $\hat{F}(1000) \approx 0.62$ means that about $62\%$ of workers earn at most $1000$ dollars per month.
Inverting the ECDF gives $1000$ as the $0.62$ quantile.^[
The option `type=1` directly inverts the ECDF, whereas R's default interpolates between observations.
Newcomers may find the command `quantile(X, probs=.62, type=1)` easier to learn, and it gives the same answer as `quantile(F_hat, probs=.62, type=1)` since `F_hat` is built from the sorted data.]

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Proportion of Data <= 1000
mean(X <= 1000) # Direct calculation
F_hat(1000)     # using the ECDF
# Value of x at which 62% of data are <= x
quantile(F_hat, probs=.62, type=1)  # Invert the ECDF
```

The plot gives approximate readings of these values.
The blue line runs from $0.62$ on the vertical axis to the ECDF.
It then drops to $1000$ on the horizontal axis.
Following the line from $1000$ gives $0.62$.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
# ECDF of monthly earnings
plot(F_hat, main=NA, pch=16, col=grey(0, .5),
    xlab='Monthly earnings (1980 dollars)',
    ylab='Proportion of workers at or below x')
# Blue line from 0.62 across to the ECDF, then down to 1000
segments(-500, 0.62, 1000, 0.62, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8))
segments(1000, 0, 1000, 0.62, col=rgb(0, 0, 1, .8))
```


**Things to try.**

* Estimate the median from the figure and check it numerically.
* Evaluate `F_hat` below the smallest observation and above the largest.
* Move the vertical line to the upper quartile with `quantile(F_hat, probs=.75, type=1)`.
* Repeat the code for `X <- c(2, 3.1, 0.01)` and check each result by hand.

# Bootstrap

### What {-}

A bootstrap sample draws $n$ observations from the data with replacement.
Each observation has probability $1/n$ of being selected on each draw.
These draws come from $\hat{F}$.^[
Part 1 inverted $\hat{F}$ at $p=0.62$ to get $1000$.
Inverting $\hat{F}$ at a random $p$ also gives a random draw from $\hat{F}$.
The command `quantile(F_hat, probs=runif(1), type=1)` does this, and has the same distribution as `sample(X, 1)`.
]
```{r}
#| eval: true
# single random draw from F_hat
sample(X, 1) 
```
A statistic is computed for each of $B$ bootstrap samples.
These values form the bootstrap distribution.
```{r}
#| eval: true
# Bootstrap sample
X_1 <- sample(X, replace=TRUE)
median(X_1)
# Another Bootstrap sample
X_2 <- sample(X, replace=TRUE)
median(X_2)
```



### Why {-}

The standard error formula for a median is beyond an introductory course, but the bootstrap loop does not need a formula.
The bootstrap distribution approximates the statistic's sampling distribution because $\hat{F} \approx F$.
Its middle $95\%$ gives the percentile confidence interval.

The same approach works for the `mean`, and is often more intuitive.
Students can inspect each step in the loop with real data.
The same intuition they build generalizes to other statistics.

### How {-}

The sample median is $905$ dollars per month.
The bootstrap estimates how much this median would vary across samples of 935 workers.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| output: false
# Number of bootstrap samples
B <- 9999
# Empty vector to hold the bootstrap medians
boot_medians <- rep(NA, B)
# Fill the vector in a loop
for (b in 1:B) {
    # Resample the data with replacement, then store the median
    X_b <- sample(X, replace=TRUE)
    boot_medians[b] <- median(X_b)
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Percentile confidence interval: the middle 95% of bootstrap medians
boot_ci <- quantile(boot_medians, probs=c(.025, .975))
boot_ci

# Histogram of bootstrap medians, with the interval in blue
hist(boot_medians, main=NA, xlab='Bootstrap median')
abline(v=boot_ci, col='blue', lwd=2)
```

Each pass through the loop draws 935 rows *with replacement*.
Some workers appear more than once.
Others do not appear.
The loop stores the median of each resample.
The middle $95\%$ of these medians gives the confidence interval.

**Things to try.**

* Test two hypothesized values inside the interval and two outside it.
* Change `median(X_b)` to `mean(X_b)` in the loop and re-run.
* Change `probs=c(.025, .975)` to `probs=c(.05, .95)` and confirm that the interval narrows.
* Compare the percentile interval with the normal-approximation interval printed next in the script.
* Repeat the ECDF and bootstrap exercises with `ceosal1[, 'salary']` from the `wooldridge` package.^[
Like `wage2`, these data are a sample of individuals.
Many economists compute standard errors with population level datasets, but this is not a habit I would want to encourage.
Set `X <- wooldridge::ceosal1[, 'salary']`.
]

# Scripting and AI

Save your work as `ECDF_Bootstrap.R`.
If you did not follow along, use the version I created.

Close RStudio and open the saved script.
The script records the steps in the analysis.

It also gives an AI assistant something to review.
The `wage2` data are public and contain no names or other identifying information.
The script is safe to upload.

### Step 1: write comments {-}

Write three sentences at the top of the script.
Summarize the main statistical ideas.

Change one comment to misdescribe its code.
For example, change "middle 95%" to "middle 90%", or "with replacement" to "without replacement".
Write down the line number.

### Step 2: upload and ask about the comments {-}

Open a new chat at [claude.ai](https://claude.ai).
Attach `ECDF_Bootstrap.R` with the attach button in the message box.
Then send this prompt.

> This R script is from an introductory statistics course.
> I wrote the comments.
> Check whether they describe the code correctly.

Then send this prompt.

> Identify any bugs in the code.
> Check the accuracy of my summary.

Check whether Claude found the incorrect comment.
Check whether it flagged any correct code or comments as errors.

### Step 3: ask your own questions {-}

Ask about an unclear part of the lab in your own words.
Then ask Claude to complete an exercise.
For example:

> Update the script to bootstrap the mean.
> Construct a 90% confidence interval and check it against the formula.

Save the new script as `ECDF_Bootstrap_ClaudeV1.R`.
Open it in RStudio and check that it works.

### Step 4: convert it to Quarto {-}

> Convert this R script to a Quarto document that renders to HTML.
> Name the file `ECDF_Bootstrap_ClaudeV1.qmd`.
> Keep the content unchanged.

In RStudio, open the file and click *Render*.

# Extensions

## The Fundamental Theorem of Statistics

### What {-}

The population CDF is $F(x) = \text{Prob}(X \leq x)$.
The book introduces it as the ECDF of an infinite dataset.
The Glivenko-Cantelli theorem is also called the Fundamental Theorem of Statistics.
As $n$ grows, the largest vertical gap between $\hat{F}$ and $F$ shrinks to zero.
$$\sup_x \left| \hat{F}(x) - F(x) \right| \rightarrow 0.$$

### Why {-}

The share of workers earning at most $1000$ dollars in Part 1 is $\hat{F}(1000)$.
The theorem supports using it to estimate $F(1000)$.
It also explains the use of $\hat{F}$ in the bootstrap.
A draw from $\hat{F}$ approximates a draw from $F$.
The next two plots illustrate convergence.

### How {-}

The simulation uses a known population CDF.
The code below uses log-normal household incomes with a median of exactly $50{,}000$.

```{r}
#| eval: true
# Log-normal incomes with a median of 50,000
income_meanlog <- log(50000)
income_sdlog <- 0.6
# Population CDF, F(x)
F_pop <- function(x) plnorm(x, meanlog=income_meanlog, sdlog=income_sdlog)
# Random sample of n incomes from the population
r_pop <- function(n) rlnorm(n, meanlog=income_meanlog, sdlog=income_sdlog)
```

The function `F_pop` gives the population CDF $F$.
The function `r_pop` draws random samples from this population.

The three panels use samples of 10, 100, and 1000 observations.
Grey steps show each sample's ECDF.
The red curve shows the population CDF.
Larger samples produce smaller steps and closer agreement with the population CDF.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.5
# Draw the population CDF over many specific x
x_grid <- seq(0, 200000, length.out=500)
F_grid <- F_pop(x_grid)
# Three panels side by side, one per sample size
par(mfrow=c(1, 3))
for (n_sim in c(10, 100, 1000)) {
    # Draw one sample and plot its ECDF
    X_sim <- r_pop(n_sim)
    F_hat <- ecdf(X_sim)
    plot(F_hat, main=NA, xlim=c(0, 200000),
        xlab='Income', ylab='Proportion at or below x')
    # Add the population CDF in red
    lines(x_grid, F_grid, col="red", lwd=2)
    title(paste0('n = ', n_sim), font.main=1)
}
```

The second figure shows 30 sample ECDFs in each panel.
Each grey curve comes from a separate sample.
The population CDF is omitted.
The spread of the curves shows variation across samples.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.5
# Number of samples in each panel
n_spaghetti <- 30
# Three panels side by side, one per sample size
par(mfrow=c(1, 3))
for (n_sim in c(10, 100, 1000)) {
    # Empty plot to draw the ECDFs on
    plot(NA, xlim=c(0, 200000), ylim=c(0, 1),
        xlab='Income', ylab='Proportion at or below x')
    for (i in seq_len(n_spaghetti)) {
        # Draw a new sample and add its ECDF
        X_sim <- r_pop(n_sim)
        F_hat <- ecdf(X_sim)
        lines(F_hat, col=grey(0, .15), do.points=FALSE)
    }
    title(paste0('n = ', n_sim), font.main=1)
}
```

At $n = 10$, the ECDFs differ substantially.
At $n = 1000$, they lie close together and close to $F$.
The plot illustrates the convergence described by the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem.

**Things to try.**

* Re-run the three-panel loop a few times.
  The $n = 10$ panel changes substantially.
  The $n = 1000$ panel changes little.
* Replace the log-normal draws with `runif()` or `rexp()`.
  Update `F_pop` to match.
  The ECDF still converges to the population CDF.
* Raise `n_spaghetti` to 100 and make the curves more transparent with `grey(0, .05)`.
  More curves make the variation across samples easier to see.

## More extensions

You can adapt this document for your courses.
Additional material is openly available online.

* [Data (Ch. 2)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/01_02_Data.html), Exercises: the ECDF of `Assault` and the share of states at or below 200.
* [Intervals (Ch. 7)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/01_07_Intervals.html), Exercise 4: a bootstrap $95\%$ interval for the median of `UrbanPop`.
* [Two Groups (Ch. 12)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/02_12_TwoGroups.html): ECDFs by group and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic.
* [Data Analysis (Ch. 20)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/02_20_DataAnalysis.html): reproducible reporting with Quarto.
* [Working with AI (Appendix A)](https://jadamso.github.io/Rbooks/04_A_WorkingWithAI.html): the full eight-step review.
